records.title: Malignant spinal cord compression
records.subtitle: Structural
records.body: Epidural tumour compressing cord or cauda equina — new/worsening back pain, leg weakness, sensory level, or bladder/bowel change in a cancer patient. Ambulant function is the clock: treat before it is lost. Dexamethasone 16 mg (oral or equivalent IV) as soon as MSCC is suspected — with PPI cover; do not wait for imaging. Whole-spine MRI within 24 h (CT with contrast if MRI contraindicated) — image the whole spine, lesions are often multilevel. Flat bed rest / spinal precautions until stability is assessed. Refer same-day to oncology + spinal surgery / radiation oncology; assess ambulatory status and document it (it drives prognosis). Recognise Suspect early. Back pain (often the first symptom, may precede neurology by weeks; worse on lying, straining, or at night), progressing to limb weakness, a sensory level, gait disturbance, and — later — urinary retention / incontinence and reduced anal tone. Thoracic spine is the commonest site. Speed of onset matters. A motor deficit evolving over <24–48 h carries a worse prognosis and demands faster diagnosis than a deficit creeping over >7 days. Autonomic (bladder/bowel) signs are late — do not wait for them. Commonest primaries: breast, prostate, lung, myeloma, renal. Confirm Whole-spine MRI within 24 h of suspected MSCC is the investigation of choice; whole-spine CT with contrast if MRI is contraindicated or unavailable. Image the entire spine — cord compression is multilevel in roughly a third of cases, and the plan changes if there is a second site. Establish tissue diagnosis where the primary is unknown, but never let the biopsy delay steroids or definitive treatment in a threatened cord. Manage Corticosteroid: dexamethasone 16 mg (oral or equivalent parenteral) as soon as MSCC is suspected, then 16 mg daily while awaiting surgery or radiotherapy, with gastric protection and glucose monitoring; taper once definitive treatment is under way. Stop it if imaging excludes MSCC. (A 10 mg IV loading bolus is common practice but is not part of the NICE regimen.) Definitive treatment — surgery vs radiotherapy: decompressive surgery followed by radiotherapy preserved and restored walking better than radiotherapy alone in the Patchell RCT (able to walk after treatment 84% vs 57%; among those non-ambulant at entry, regained walking 62% vs 19%). Favour surgery for a single area of compression, spinal instability, an unknown primary needing tissue, radioresistant histology, or deficit despite/after prior RT — in patients fit for it with a reasonable prognosis. Radiotherapy for those not surgical candidates, radiosensitive tumours, multilevel disease, or poor performance status. Systemic therapy can be first-line for exquisitely chemo/hormone-sensitive disease (e.g. lymphoma, germ cell, some prostate) alongside the above. Bladder care (catheterise retention), VTE prophylaxis, pressure-area and bowel care, analgesia. Disposition & escalation Admit; discuss same-day with spinal surgery and radiation oncology (many centres run an MSCC coordinator / pathway). Pre-treatment ambulatory status is the strongest predictor of walking afterwards — patients treated while still walking usually stay walking; once paraplegic, few recover. This is what makes the 24 h window real. Definitive treatment ideally within 24 h of the diagnosis in a threatened cord. Pitfalls Waiting for bladder/bowel signs — by then the cord is often lost. Imaging only the symptomatic level and missing higher compression. Withholding steroids pending MRI, or omitting gastric/glucose cover. Referring the day after, not the hour of, suspicion. Related: raised ICP & brain-met crises (this module) for the parallel steroid-for-oedema logic; bone-metastasis and primary-tumour management sit in the wiki. NICE NG234 Spinal metastases and metastatic spinal cord compression (2023) · Patchell RA et al, Lancet 2005;366:643–648 (DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(05)66954-1; PMID 16112300). ESMO Handbook ch. 7.

records.title: Superior vena cava obstruction
records.subtitle: Structural
records.body: Obstruction of SVC flow — facial/neck/arm swelling, distended neck and chest-wall veins, dyspnoea, plethora; commonly lung cancer or lymphoma. Urgency is set by airway and cerebral signs, not the cosmetic swelling. Assess for the red flags — stridor / airway compromise, or cerebral signs (confusion, reduced consciousness, visual change from laryngeal/cerebral oedema). These make it an emergency. Sit the patient up; give oxygen. Get tissue first unless airway/cerebral compromise forces the hand — the treatment depends entirely on the histology. Endovascular stenting for severe or life-threatening (Yale grade 3–4) obstruction — fastest relief, and it does not need a diagnosis. Recognise Facial and neck swelling, dyspnoea and a sensation of fullness, distended neck and chest-wall collateral veins, facial plethora, cough; worse on bending forward or lying flat. Onset is usually gradual (collaterals develop), so most presentations are urgent rather than immediately life-threatening. The dangerous minority: stridor or airway oedema, and cerebral oedema (headache, confusion, obtundation) — a rapidly occluding SVC that has outrun its collaterals. These override the usual biopsy-first rule. Malignant causes dominate — non-small-cell and small-cell lung cancer, non-Hodgkin lymphoma; also consider catheter/device-associated thrombosis. Confirm Contrast CT of the thorax defines the level, extent and cause of obstruction and guides both biopsy and stenting. Secure a histological diagnosis (sputum/pleural cytology, nodal or bronchoscopic biopsy, image-guided core) before treatment — management is entirely disease-specific, and treating blind can forfeit a curable-intent diagnosis (e.g. lymphoma, small-cell, germ cell). Manage Endovascular stenting gives the most rapid symptom relief and is the treatment of choice for severe or life-threatening SVCO; it is independent of histology, so it can precede the diagnosis when symptoms are urgent. Tumour-directed therapy by histology: chemotherapy (± the stent) for chemosensitive disease — small-cell lung cancer, lymphoma, germ cell; radiotherapy for non-small-cell lung cancer and other less chemosensitive tumours. Anticoagulation if the obstruction is thrombotic or a stent is placed (per local protocol). Corticosteroids: often given, but the evidence is weak and benefit uncertain outside steroid-responsive tumours (lymphoma) or to limit a radiotherapy-associated oedema flare — not a substitute for definitive treatment. Head elevation and oxygen are supportive only. Grade — Yale (Yu) system G0 radiographic obstruction, asymptomatic. G1 mild — head/neck oedema, plethora, cyanosis. G2 moderate — oedema with functional impairment (mild dysphagia, cough, mild visual disturbance). G3 severe — cerebral oedema (mild headache, dizziness) or laryngeal oedema, or diminished cardiac reserve (syncope on bending). G4 life-threatening — significant cerebral oedema (confusion, obtundation) or laryngeal oedema (stridor), or significant haemodynamic compromise. G5 fatal. Grade 3–4 is the threshold that pushes urgent stenting ahead of the biopsy. Disposition & escalation Grade 3–4 (airway or cerebral signs, haemodynamic compromise) → monitored bed, urgent interventional radiology for stenting, anaesthetic/ITU input for a threatened airway. Grade 1–2 → expedited work-up to tissue diagnosis then disease-specific treatment; genuine emergencies are the minority. Pitfalls Empirical radiotherapy before biopsy — it can render a lymphoma or small-cell unclassifiable and lose curative-intent treatment. Treating SVCO as uniformly life-threatening: most is urgent, not peri-arrest — let the airway/cerebral signs, not the facial swelling, set the pace. Missing catheter-associated thrombus as the cause. Yu JB, Wilson LD, Detterbeck FC, J Thorac Oncol 2008;3:811–814 (Yale/Yu classification & management algorithm; PMID 18670297). ESMO Handbook ch. 3.

records.title: Cardiac tamponade / malignant pericardial effusion
records.subtitle: Structural
records.body: Pericardial fluid raising intrapericardial pressure and choking cardiac filling — obstructive shock. Dyspnoea, tachycardia, hypotension, raised JVP in a cancer patient; can arrest as PEA. Echocardiography now — it makes the diagnosis (effusion + diastolic RV/RA collapse, IVC plethora) and guides drainage. Recognise decompensation: hypotension, tachycardia, raised JVP (Beck's triad), pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory SBP fall >10 mmHg). Urgent (echo-guided) pericardiocentesis for haemodynamic compromise — the definitive move; do not delay for a full oncological work-up. Bridge with IV fluids while preparing to drain; avoid intubation / positive-pressure ventilation if possible — it can precipitate arrest in a tamponade. Recognise Progressive dyspnoea, orthopnoea, fatigue, chest discomfort; on examination tachycardia, hypotension, raised JVP, quiet heart sounds and pulsus paradoxus. Beck's triad (hypotension, muffled sounds, distended neck veins) is specific but insensitive — the full triad is uncommon and its absence does not exclude tamponade. Tamponade is a physiological diagnosis: it is the haemodynamic effect, not the effusion size, that defines it — a rapidly accumulating small effusion can tampon where a large chronic one does not. Common in advanced lung and breast cancer, lymphoma, melanoma; also radiation pericarditis and, rarely, immunotherapy-related. Confirm Echocardiography is the single most useful test: it confirms the effusion, sizes it, and shows the tamponade physiology (diastolic collapse of the right atrium then right ventricle, a plethoric non-collapsing IVC, respirophasic transvalvular flow variation). Effusion size by echo in diastole: mild <10 mm, moderate 10–20 mm, large >20 mm. ECG may show low voltages and electrical alternans; chest X-ray a globular heart. Send drained fluid for cytology. Manage Pericardiocentesis (echo-guided, or fluoroscopic) is indicated for tamponade and for symptomatic large effusions or suspected neoplastic aetiology; it is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Leave a catheter for extended drainage — it markedly cuts re-accumulation versus a single tap. Temporising while you set up: IV fluid to support preload; vasopressor if needed. Avoid positive-pressure ventilation where you can — it drops venous return and can tip a compensated tamponade into arrest. Prevent recurrence: extended catheter drainage, or a surgical pericardial window (subxiphoid or thoracoscopic) for recurrent/loculated effusions; intrapericardial sclerosing/cytotoxic agents are an option but cause chest pain and constriction and are used selectively. Treat the cancer: systemic antineoplastic therapy for the underlying malignancy is the durable control. Disposition & escalation Monitored bed / HDU–ICU; involve cardiology and cardiothoracic surgery. Recurrence guides the escalation ladder: after isolated pericardiocentesis re-accumulation is common (~38% in pooled series), versus roughly 10–12% with extended catheter drainage, sclerosis or balloon pericardiotomy, and under ~7% after a surgical window — so a recurrent malignant effusion is a window/extended-drainage problem, not a repeat-tap one. Pitfalls Anchoring on effusion size — a small, fast effusion can tampon; a large slow one may not. Intubating a hypotensive tamponade before drainage — risk of periarrest. Aggressive diuresis / vasodilators — they cut preload and worsen the obstruction. Single tap and discharge in malignant disease — plan for re-accumulation. 2015 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases, Eur Heart J 2015;36:2921–2964 (PMID 26320112) · malignant pericardial effusion recurrence rates from pooled observational data (systematic review, PMC11357784). ESMO Handbook ch. 1.

records.title: Raised intracranial pressure & brain-metastasis crises
records.subtitle: Structural
records.body: Mass effect / vasogenic oedema (or haemorrhage) from brain metastases raising ICP — headache, vomiting, drowsiness, focal deficit, seizure; herniation is the peri-arrest end. Recognise herniation: falling GCS, new pupillary asymmetry / fixed dilated pupil, Cushing response (hypertension + bradycardia), abnormal posturing — a neurosurgical emergency. Airway/breathing first; nurse head-up ~30°, head midline; treat hypoxia and hypercapnia. Dexamethasone for vasogenic oedema — up to 16 mg/day for severe raised-ICP symptoms (4–8 mg/day suffices for milder mass-effect symptoms); with PPI cover. For impending herniation: hyperosmolar therapy — mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg IV over 15–30 min, or 3% hypertonic saline — and call neurosurgery now . Recognise Raised-ICP syndrome: headache (worse on waking, coughing, lying flat), nausea and vomiting, progressive drowsiness, papilloedema, and evolving focal deficits. Seizures may be the presentation. Herniation red flags — declining consciousness, a new dilated/unreactive pupil, the Cushing response (hypertension with bradycardia), and extensor posturing — mark decompensation and demand immediate action. Sudden deterioration suggests intratumoural haemorrhage (melanoma, renal, choriocarcinoma, thyroid) or obstructive hydrocephalus. Confirm Urgent CT head (with contrast, or MRI where feasible) for the number, size and site of metastases, midline shift, hydrocephalus and haemorrhage. Do not let imaging delay hyperosmolar therapy or the neurosurgical call in a herniating patient — treat and scan in parallel. Manage Corticosteroid (vasogenic oedema): dexamethasone — 4–8 mg/day for mild-to-moderate mass-effect symptoms, up to 16 mg/day for severe or raised-ICP symptoms; higher doses add toxicity without extra benefit in less-severe disease, so reserve them. Steroids are not indicated for asymptomatic metastases. Give gastric protection and monitor glucose; taper to the minimum effective dose. (A 10 mg IV loading bolus is common practice but is not a fixed guideline figure.) Hyperosmolar therapy (herniation / critical ICP): mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg IV over 15–30 min, or 3% hypertonic saline as an alternative — a bridge to definitive decompression, not a treatment on its own. Seizures: treat active seizures (benzodiazepine → load an antiepileptic); do not give prophylactic antiepileptics to seizure-free patients with brain metastases — routine prophylaxis is not recommended. Definitive control: urgent neurosurgery (resection of a dominant/haemorrhagic lesion; CSF diversion for hydrocephalus) and/or radiotherapy (SRS for limited disease, whole-brain in selected cases); systemic therapy where the disease is exquisitely responsive. Airway protection, head-up positioning, normocapnia; brief controlled hyperventilation only as a short bridge to theatre. Disposition & escalation Herniation or critically raised ICP → immediate neurosurgical referral, ICU/HDU, airway management. Stabilise oedema with steroids and decide definitive local therapy (surgery/RT) with neuro-oncology and radiation oncology, weighted to performance status, systemic disease burden and prognosis. Pitfalls Prophylactic antiepileptics in a seizure-free patient — no benefit, real interactions and toxicity. Reflex high-dose 16 mg dexamethasone for every patient — match the dose to symptom severity; over-steroiding causes myopathy, hyperglycaemia, infection. Relying on mannitol/hyperventilation as anything more than a bridge to surgical decompression. Missing intratumoural haemorrhage or hydrocephalus as the cause of sudden deterioration. Related: MSCC (this module) shares the steroid-for-oedema logic; immunotherapy-related neurotoxicity and its steroid dosing sit in Tox. Chang SM et al (Congress of Neurological Surgeons; ASCO/SNO endorsement), J Clin Oncol 2019;37:1130–1135 — anticonvulsant prophylaxis & steroid use in metastatic brain tumours (DOI 10.1200/JCO.18.02085) · hyperosmolar dosing per Neurocritical Care Society Emergency Neurological Life Support (ICP/herniation). ESMO Handbook ch. 8.

records.title: Malignant central airway obstruction / stridor
records.subtitle: Structural
records.body: Tumour narrowing the trachea or main bronchi (intraluminal or extrinsic) → positional dyspnoea, stridor, monophonic wheeze; a compensated airway can close abruptly. Sit the patient up; high-flow humidified O₂; heliox (helium–oxygen) to ease flow through the stenosis while definitive treatment is arranged. High-dose corticosteroid for peritumoural oedema; nebulised adrenaline as a temporising measure. Call interventional pulmonology / ENT and anaesthesia now — definitive relief is urgent rigid bronchoscopy with debulking ± stenting. Do not sedate, paralyse, or lie the patient flat before the airway is controlled. Recognise Stridor (fixed intrathoracic obstruction may give expiratory stridor / monophonic wheeze), exertional then positional dyspnoea, cough, haemoptysis. Usually central lung, thyroid, oesophageal or mediastinal-nodal disease — intraluminal tumour, extrinsic compression, or both. Peri-arrest signs: exhaustion, accessory-muscle use, a quiet chest, falling SpO₂ with rising CO₂. Confirm In the decompensating patient, do not delay the interventional call for imaging. When stable: flexible nasendoscopy / bronchoscopy defines the level and whether it is intrinsic vs extrinsic; CT neck–thorax maps the lesion and distal airway patency; a flow–volume loop shows the obstruction pattern. Manage Temporise: sit up, heliox (lower gas density improves laminar flow past a fixed narrowing), high-flow humidified O₂, high-dose corticosteroid for oedema, nebulised adrenaline. Definitive — rigid bronchoscopy is the workhorse: mechanical debulking, laser or cryo for intraluminal tumour; self-expanding or silicone stent for extrinsic compression. Flexible bronchoscopy for adjuncts only. Consolidate: external-beam radiotherapy (or endobronchial brachytherapy) for radiosensitive tumour once the airway is secured; systemic therapy for chemosensitive disease. Securing the airway: inhalational / awake technique with the interventionalist and rigid scope in the room; avoid routine paralysis or supine positioning, which can precipitate complete obstruction. Disposition & escalation Peri-arrest → theatre / bronchoscopy suite with thoracic-surgery or ENT + anaesthesia; HDU / ICU afterwards. Central airway obstruction usually marks advanced disease — agree a ceiling of care early, before the crash. Pitfalls Sedation, muscle relaxant, or lying the patient flat before the airway is controlled. Labelling the stridor as "asthma / COPD" and reaching for bronchodilators alone. Waiting on imaging in a decompensating patient instead of calling the interventionalist. CHEST expert panel, Management of Central Airway Obstruction , Chest 2024 · Mudambi et al, J Thorac Dis 2017 (overview of malignant CAO). ESMO Handbook ch. 13 (Dyspnoea and Respiratory Failure).

records.title: Malignant bowel obstruction
records.subtitle: Structural
records.body: Mechanical or functional obstruction from intra-abdominal / peritoneal malignancy (commonly ovarian, colorectal) → colicky pain, vomiting, distension, absolute constipation. "Drip and suck": nil by mouth, wide-bore NG tube on free drainage, IV crystalloid; correct hypokalaemia / hyponatraemia. Analgesia (opioid) and antiemetic (haloperidol); stop prokinetics if there is colic or complete obstruction. Anti-secretory — hyoscine butylbromide 60–120 mg/24h CSCI, or octreotide 300–600 µg/24h SC/CSCI. Dexamethasone 6–16 mg/day IV (may hasten resolution); early joint surgical + oncology review. Recognise Colicky or constant abdominal pain, vomiting (faeculent when distal), distension, absolute constipation. Separate mechanical obstruction from functional causes (opioids, hypokalaemia), and single-level from multi-level disease — it drives whether surgery or a stent can help. Confirm Examine for localised tenderness / peritonism (strangulation or perforation). FBC, U&E — correct potassium and sodium. Erect chest / abdominal film, then CT abdomen–pelvis to fix the level and cause, single vs multi-level, and to triage surgery vs stent vs medical palliation. Manage Decompress & resuscitate: NBM, NG free drainage, IV crystalloid, correct electrolytes. Symptom control (CSCI): analgesia (morphine / diamorphine); antiemetic — haloperidol first-line, or cyclizine / levomepromazine; anti-secretory — hyoscine butylbromide 60–120 mg/24h or octreotide 300–600 µg/24h (up to ~800); corticosteroid — dexamethasone 6–16 mg/day IV, which may bring about resolution. Metoclopramide only in incomplete obstruction without colic — prokinesis worsens colic and is contraindicated in complete obstruction. Definitive: surgery (bypass / resection / stoma) for fit patients with a single correctable mechanical level; self-expanding metallic stent for obstructing left-colonic or gastroduodenal lesions; medical palliation where surgery is inappropriate (diffuse peritoneal disease, poor performance status). Disposition & escalation Joint surgical / oncology / palliative-care decision — the choice is as much prognostic as technical. Venting gastrostomy for refractory vomiting when a long-term NG tube is unacceptable. Pitfalls Missing strangulation / perforation (fever, peritonism, rising lactate) behind a label of "inoperable obstruction". Prokinetics in complete obstruction or colic. Committing to "medical only" without CT — a single reversible level may be surgically or stent-correctable. MASCC evidence-based recommendations, medical management of MBO (2021 update), Support Care Cancer · Feuer & Broadley, Cochrane 2000 (corticosteroids, CD001219) · Ripamonti et al, Support Care Cancer 2000 (hyoscine butylbromide) · Mercadante octreotide RCTs. ESMO Handbook ch. 16 (Obstructive Bowel Disease).

records.title: Obstructive uropathy & urological emergencies
records.subtitle: Structural
records.body: Malignant ureteric obstruction (pelvic / retroperitoneal tumour or nodes) → AKI, anuria, hyperkalaemia; or haemorrhagic cystitis with clot retention. Bilateral obstruction with AKI / anuria or urosepsis → urgent decompression : percutaneous nephrostomy or retrograde ureteric stent — do not wait. Check U&E and potassium; treat hyperkalaemia immediately. Haemorrhagic cystitis: 3-way catheter with continuous bladder irrigation, evacuate clots — mesna is prophylaxis, not treatment . Renal-tract ultrasound (hydronephrosis) ± CT; involve urology now; anticipate post-obstructive diuresis after relief. Recognise Obstructive uropathy: bilateral ureteric obstruction — or obstruction of a single functioning kidney — from pelvic / retroperitoneal tumour or nodal disease → AKI, anuria; hyperkalaemia and uraemia are what kill. Haemorrhagic cystitis: visible haematuria / clot retention after cyclophosphamide or ifosfamide (acrolein toxicity), pelvic radiotherapy, or BK / adenovirus in the immunosuppressed. Confirm U&E, potassium, venous gas. Renal-tract ultrasound for hydronephrosis ± non-contrast CT for level and cause. Catheterise for retention or clot. If bleeding: FBC, coagulation, group & save. Manage Decompress obstruction: percutaneous nephrostomy or retrograde ureteric stent — nephrostomy is often preferred in malignant obstruction for higher technical success; stent where feasible. Treat hyperkalaemia and uraemic complications in parallel; dialysis if refractory. Haemorrhagic cystitis: 3-way catheter with continuous bladder irrigation, manual / cystoscopic clot evacuation. Prophylaxis for ifosfamide (and high-dose cyclophosphamide) is hyperhydration plus mesna — total 60–100% of the oxazaphosphorine dose, e.g. 20% IV at 0, +4 and +8 h. Refractory bleeding → intravesical agents, cystoscopic diathermy, or arterial embolisation. Post-obstructive diuresis: after relieving bilateral obstruction, monitor urine output and replace fluid and electrolytes — losses can be profound. Disposition & escalation Urology plus nephrology. In advanced disease, weigh whether decompression fits the goals of care — a nephrostomy in end-stage malignant obstruction warrants an honest conversation about what it buys. Pitfalls Discharging an anuric patient with bilateral obstruction — hyperkalaemia is rapidly fatal. Giving mesna as treatment for established cystitis (it is prophylaxis only). Under-replacing post-obstructive diuresis. ESMO Handbook ch. 9 (Renal Failure and Urological Emergencies) · ASCO chemotherapy uroprotectant guideline (Hensley et al, JCO 2009) for mesna dosing · urological-emergency reviews.

records.title: Tumour lysis syndrome
records.subtitle: Metabolic
records.body: Massive tumour-cell turnover → hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hyperuricaemia, hypocalcaemia ± AKI; peri-treatment in bulky / high-turnover disease. Aggressive isotonic IV fluids (~2500–3000 mL/m²/day; target urine output ≥2 mL/kg/h). Rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg IV for high-risk / established disease — hold if G6PD-deficient . Continuous cardiac monitoring; treat hyperkalaemia immediately. Bloods q4–6h (urate, K, PO₄, Ca, creatinine, LDH); involve nephrology early. Recognise Cairo–Bishop. Laboratory TLS = ≥2 of the following, from 3 days before to 7 days after therapy: uric acid ≥476 µmol/L (8 mg/dL) · K⁺ ≥6.0 mmol/L · phosphate ≥1.45 mmol/L (adults) · corrected Ca²⁺ ≤1.75 mmol/L. Clinical TLS = laboratory TLS + one of: AKI (creatinine ≥1.5×ULN), cardiac arrhythmia / sudden death, or seizure. Howard (2011) refinements: require the two abnormalities simultaneously ; the original 25%-change-from-baseline criterion is dropped (rarely meaningful unless already out of range); any symptomatic hypocalcaemia counts as clinical TLS. Highest risk: Burkitt / lymphoblastic lymphoma, ALL and AML with high WBC, bulky chemosensitive tumours; compounded by pre-existing renal impairment, volume depletion, high LDH / urate. Confirm Urate, K, phosphate, corrected calcium, creatinine, LDH; ECG / telemetry; urine output. Monitoring cadence: high-risk q4–6h · intermediate q8–12h · low-risk daily, through the at-risk period (regimen-dependent). Manage Risk-stratified prophylaxis: low → allopurinol 300 mg/day + hydration; intermediate → allopurinol + hydration (rasburicase if urate climbs); high / established → rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg IV daily + aggressive hydration. Do not combine allopurinol with rasburicase (allopurinol starves rasburicase of substrate). Fluids: isotonic hyperhydration ~2500–3000 mL/m²/day (highest risk), target urine output ≥2 mL/kg/h; avoid routine urinary alkalinisation (worsens calcium-phosphate precipitation, especially when rasburicase is available); loop diuretic if urine output stays low despite optimal hydration. Hyperkalaemia: calcium gluconate for cardioprotection, insulin–dextrose, salbutamol, binders; dialysis if refractory. Hyperphosphataemia: phosphate binders. Hypocalcaemia: treat only if symptomatic — giving calcium against a high phosphate risks metastatic calcification. Grade No true severity ladder — Cairo–Bishop distinguishes laboratory from clinical TLS (clinical = organ involvement); Howard 2011 offers a 0–IV clinical grade. Disposition & escalation High-risk patients → monitored bed / HDU. Renal replacement therapy for refractory hyperkalaemia, severe hyperphosphataemia / symptomatic hypocalcaemia, fluid overload, or oliguric AKI → nephrology / ICU (lower thresholds than for other AKI). Where feasible, control urate before cytoreduction in very-high-risk disease. Pitfalls Rasburicase in G6PD deficiency (haemolysis, methaemoglobinaemia) — screen high-risk ancestry first. After rasburicase, uric-acid samples must go on ice or they degrade ex vivo (falsely low). Over-alkalinisation. Treating asymptomatic hypocalcaemia. Cairo & Bishop, Br J Haematol 2004 · Coiffier et al, JCO 2008 (TLS expert panel) · Howard et al, NEJM 2011 · British Society for Haematology (Jones et al) 2015 · NCCN. ESMO Handbook ch. 11.

records.title: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy
records.subtitle: Metabolic
records.body: The commonest life-threatening metabolic emergency in cancer — usually PTHrP-driven (humoral) or osteolytic; dehydration, confusion, constipation, polyuria, AKI. Severity tracks the corrected calcium and the symptoms, not either alone. Confirm on corrected calcium (or ionised Ca); ECG (short QT, bradyarrhythmia). Rehydrate first: 0.9% saline IV ~200–500 mL/h to volume status — the immediate priority. Zoledronic acid 4 mg IV over ≥15 min once rehydrated (reduce/withhold in renal impairment; denosumab if bisphosphonate-refractory or CrCl <30). Calcitonin 4 units/kg SC/IM q12h for rapid short-term lowering while the bisphosphonate takes effect. Recognise Suspect in any cancer patient with new confusion, dehydration, constipation, polyuria/polydipsia or AKI. Symptoms track the rate of rise as much as the level. Severity (corrected Ca): mild <3.0 mmol/L · moderate 3.0–3.4 · severe >3.4 mmol/L (or symptomatic at any level) — severe / symptomatic is the emergency. Mechanism steers treatment: humoral (PTHrP, most solid tumours) · osteolytic (myeloma, breast) · 1,25-dihydroxy-vitamin-D-mediated (lymphoma, granulomatous disease — the one that responds to steroids). Confirm Corrected calcium = measured total Ca + 0.02 × (40 − albumin g/L); use ionised calcium where albumin or acid–base is deranged. PTH (suppressed in malignancy — distinguishes from primary hyperparathyroidism), PTHrP, phosphate, magnesium, renal function, ECG. Add 25-OH and 1,25-OH vitamin D if the cause is unclear (lymphoma / granuloma). Manage Rehydrate first: 0.9% saline ~200–500 mL/h titrated to volume status (commonly 3–4 L over 24 h); restores GFR and drives calciuresis. Watch for overload in cardiac / renal disease. Zoledronic acid 4 mg IV over ≥15 min once volume-replete — nadir at day 4–7, effect lasts weeks. CrCl 30–60 mL/min: reduce to 3 mg; avoid if CrCl <30. Ensure hydration to limit nephrotoxicity. Denosumab 120 mg SC (repeat day 8, day 15, then monthly) for bisphosphonate-refractory hypercalcaemia or where bisphosphonate is contraindicated by renal impairment — no renal dose adjustment, but watch for delayed and sometimes profound hypocalcaemia. Calcitonin 4–8 units/kg SC/IM q6–12h for the first 24–48 h — acts within hours for a modest (~0.3–0.5 mmol/L) fall while the antiresorptive works; tachyphylaxis by 48–72 h. Loop diuretics only for fluid overload after rehydration — not a calcium-lowering measure, and harmful in a volume-depleted patient. Glucocorticoids (e.g. prednisolone 40–60 mg/day) for calcitriol-mediated hypercalcaemia of lymphoma / granulomatous disease. Dialysis for severe hypercalcaemia with renal failure or refractory to the above. Treat the malignancy — durable control needs effective anticancer therapy. Disposition & escalation Severe (>3.4 mmol/L) or symptomatic → monitored bed with telemetry and serial calcium / renal function. Nephrology for renal replacement in refractory disease or established renal failure. Recurrent hypercalcaemia signals uncontrolled disease — re-engage the treating oncology team. Pitfalls Giving a bisphosphonate before rehydrating — compounds nephrotoxicity. Reaching for a loop diuretic as first-line — worsens the dehydration that drives the calcium up. Reading an uncorrected calcium in a hypoalbuminaemic patient (falsely reassuring). Missing delayed hypocalcaemia after denosumab — check calcium and correct vitamin D / magnesium. Asonitis et al / current UK practice review, Clin Med 2023 (PMID 37775175) · zoledronic acid prescribing information (renal thresholds) · ESMO Handbook ch. 10.

records.title: Hyponatraemia / SIADH
records.subtitle: Metabolic
records.body: The commonest electrolyte disturbance in cancer; SIADH (SCLC, CNS disease, chemotherapy) is the usual euvolaemic cause. Danger tracks the rate of fall and the symptoms — and the real hazard is correcting it too fast. Grade the symptoms (seizures / obtundation / vomiting = severe) and assess volume status. Severe symptomatic: 150 mL 3% hypertonic saline IV over 20 min , recheck Na, repeat ×1–2 until symptoms settle or Na has risen 5 mmol/L. Cap the rise: ≤10 mmol/L in 24 h and ≤18 mmol/L in 48 h (≤8 mmol/L/24 h if high demyelination risk) — over-correction causes osmotic demyelination. SIADH: fluid restriction and treat the cause; send paired serum + urine osmolality and urine sodium before you touch it. Recognise Symptom severity drives urgency: severe = seizures, coma / GCS drop, vomiting, cardiorespiratory distress · moderate = nausea, confusion, headache · mild = subtle / none. Symptoms reflect how fast the sodium fell, not just how low it is. SIADH — Bartter–Schwartz criteria: clinical euvolaemia, serum osmolality <275 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg, urine sodium >30 mmol/L (on normal salt and water intake), no diuretic, and normal thyroid and adrenal function. Cancer causes: ectopic ADH (SCLC and others), CNS metastases, drugs (cyclophosphamide, vincristine, platinum), nausea, pain, opioids. Confirm Paired serum + urine osmolality and urine sodium ; glucose (exclude translocational / pseudohyponatraemia); TFTs and 9 am cortisol (hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency mimic SIADH); careful volume assessment to separate hypovolaemic, euvolaemic and hypervolaemic causes. Manage Severe / symptomatic (any sodium level): 150 mL 3% saline over 20 min (≈2 mL/kg), recheck sodium, repeat until symptoms improve or sodium has risen 5 mmol/L. Target a 5 mmol/L rise in the first hour to relieve cerebral oedema, then stop the hypertonic saline and hold within the daily limit. Correction limits: ≤10 mmol/L in the first 24 h and ≤18 mmol/L in the first 48 h. Aim lower — ≤8 mmol/L/24 h — where demyelination risk is high (sodium <105 mmol/L, hypokalaemia, alcohol-use disorder, malnutrition, advanced liver disease). If the limit is exceeded, re-lower with 5% dextrose ± desmopressin. Chronic SIADH: fluid restriction <800–1000 mL/day is first line; if inadequate add oral urea, or a vasopressin-receptor antagonist (tolvaptan) with caution — vaptans risk over-rapid correction and are hepatotoxic (avoid in liver disease and beyond 30 days). Treat the cause: systemic therapy for SCLC, withdraw the offending drug. Disposition & escalation Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia → HDU / monitored bed with sodium checked every 2–4 h during active correction. Involve endocrinology / nephrology for refractory SIADH or diagnostic uncertainty, and if over-correction needs active re-lowering. Pitfalls Correcting chronic hyponatraemia too quickly — the demyelination risk, not the low number, is what harms the patient. Starting a vaptan while fluid-restricting, or in liver disease. Labelling it SIADH without excluding hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency. Treating the sodium value rather than the patient — an asymptomatic chronic 125 mmol/L does not need hypertonic saline. Related: cerebral / leptomeningeal disease may co-drive the picture — see raised-ICP crises (this module). Spasovski et al, European clinical practice guideline on diagnosis and treatment of hyponatraemia, Eur J Endocrinol 2014;170:G1–G47 (PMID 24569125) · Verbalis et al, US expert-panel recommendations, Am J Med 2013 (PMID 24074529; high-risk ≤8 mmol/L target) · ESMO Handbook ch. 12.

records.title: Febrile neutropaenia & septic shock
records.subtitle: Infective
records.body: Fever in a neutropenic patient — a medical emergency; treat as sepsis until proven otherwise, and step up to septic-shock management the moment hypotension or hypoperfusion appears (then peri-arrest). Empiric antipseudomonal β-lactam within 1 hour — piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV, cefepime 2 g IV, or meropenem 1–2 g IV. Do not wait for the count or cultures. Draw blood cultures (peripheral + every central lumen), lactate, FBC and renal/liver panel first if it costs no time — but the antibiotic does not wait for them. If hypotensive or lactate ≥2 mmol/L: Surviving Sepsis bundle — ≥30 mL/kg crystalloid over 3 h, norepinephrine to MAP ≥65 mmHg, source control. Add vancomycin only for a specific indication (see Manage) — not routinely. Recognise Neutropenia: ANC <0.5 ×10⁹/L, or <1.0 ×10⁹/L and expected to fall below 0.5 within 48 h. Fever: a single oral temperature ≥38.3 °C, or ≥38.0 °C sustained over 1 h. One fever is the trigger — there is often no localising sign and no source. Highest risk with ANC <0.1 ×10⁹/L, anticipated neutropenia >7 days, and haematological malignancy or HSCT. Watch for the shift to septic shock: hypotension, lactate ≥2 mmol/L, mottling, new confusion. Confirm Blood cultures from a peripheral vein and from each central lumen; FBC, renal and liver panel, lactate; urinalysis, CXR and site swabs directed by symptoms. Do not delay the antibiotic for the workup. Risk-stratify (MASCC index). Score ≥21 = low risk of complications and a candidate for the oral / outpatient pathway; <21 = high risk → admit for IV therapy. The index sums burden of illness, no hypotension, no COPD, solid tumour or no prior fungal infection, no dehydration, outpatient onset, and age <60. Manage First dose within 1 h — antipseudomonal β-lactam monotherapy: piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6–8h, cefepime 2 g IV q8h, or meropenem 1–2 g IV q8h, dosed to renal function. Carbapenem first-line if a resistant organism is likely. Add vancomycin only for a named indication: haemodynamic instability / severe sepsis, suspected catheter-related infection, skin/soft-tissue infection, pneumonia, known MRSA colonisation, or Gram-positive cocci in blood pending identification. Stop at 48–72 h if not confirmed. Low risk (MASCC ≥21), stable, tolerating oral: oral ciprofloxacin + amoxicillin-clavulanate with a defined pathway for review and readmission — not if the patient was on fluoroquinolone prophylaxis. Septic shock: Surviving Sepsis bundle — ≥30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid over 3 h, norepinephrine first-line to MAP ≥65 mmHg, repeat lactate, remove an infected line. Broaden for resistant organisms and add antifungal cover if not settling. G-CSF is not routine treatment of established FN — its risk-directed use is prophylactic (see Tox). Disposition & escalation High risk (MASCC <21) → admit for IV antibiotics; profound or prolonged neutropenia → monitored bed. Shock, rising lactate, or organ dysfunction → ICU. Reassess at 48–72 h: de-escalate on culture results, continue until afebrile with a recovering ANC. Involve infection and haematology early. Pitfalls Delaying the first dose for cultures, imaging, or line access — start within the hour. Reflex vancomycin in every patient; reserve it for a named indication and stop if unconfirmed. Missing evolving shock behind a 'stable' febrile patient — recheck lactate and perfusion. Applying MASCC to an already-unstable patient; the index assumes an uncomplicated presentation. Related: G-CSF and febrile-neutropenia-risk prophylaxis are owned by Tox — Acute manages the acute episode; see Tox for primary/secondary G-CSF prophylaxis and FN-risk chemotherapy stratification. Definition, empiric therapy and vancomycin indications: Freifeld AG et al, IDSA clinical practice guideline, Clin Infect Dis 2011;52:e56–e93 (PMID 21205990). Low-risk / outpatient oral pathway: Taplitz RA et al, ASCO–IDSA guideline, J Clin Oncol 2018;36:1443–1453 (PMID 29461916). MASCC index: Klastersky J et al, J Clin Oncol 2000;18:3038–3051 (PMID 10944139). Septic shock: Evans L et al, Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021, Intensive Care Med 2021;47:1181–1247 (PMID 34599691). ESMO Handbook ch. 21.

records.title: Neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis)
records.subtitle: Infective
records.body: Fever, right-lower-quadrant / abdominal pain and diarrhoea in a neutropenic patient — inflammation and necrosis of the caecum and bowel wall; high mortality if missed. Broad-spectrum antibiotics with anaerobic and antipseudomonal Gram-negative cover — piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem (or cefepime plus metronidazole). Bowel rest, nasogastric decompression, IV fluids and electrolyte correction. Urgent CT abdomen/pelvis; serial abdominal examinations; surgical review early. No antimotility / antidiarrhoeal agents. Recognise The triad of fever, abdominal pain (classically right lower quadrant, over the caecum) and diarrhoea during neutropenia — typically 1–2 weeks after cytotoxic chemotherapy (high-dose cytarabine, taxanes, intensive induction). Distension, rebound, peritonism or GI bleeding signal transmural necrosis and impending perforation. Confirm CT abdomen/pelvis is the test of choice — circumferential bowel-wall thickening (caecum ± ascending colon), mural oedema, pericolic fat stranding, ± pneumatosis. FBC, lactate, coagulation and blood cultures; send stool for Clostridioides difficile (the key mimic). Avoid colonoscopy — perforation risk in inflamed, neutropenic bowel. Manage Antibiotics with anaerobic cover: piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6–8h or meropenem 1 g IV q8h; if using cefepime, add metronidazole for anaerobes. Add antifungal cover if not improving or persistently neutropenic. Supportive: bowel rest, nasogastric tube for ileus/obstruction, IV fluids, correction of electrolytes and coagulopathy, transfusion to target. Neutrophil recovery drives outcome — G-CSF is commonly used to shorten the neutropenic window. Avoid antimotility agents (loperamide, opioids) — they promote stasis, toxin retention and perforation. Disposition & escalation Admit to a monitored bed with serial examinations and imaging. Involve surgery early but operate selectively — surgery is reserved for perforation, uncontrolled GI bleeding, or clinical deterioration / suspected necrosis despite maximal medical therapy . Most cases resolve with neutrophil recovery and conservative care; ICU for haemodynamic instability. Pitfalls Missing it — abdominal signs are blunted in neutropenia; keep a low threshold for CT. Omitting anaerobic cover. Antimotility agents, or early colonoscopy. Not excluding C. difficile . Gorschlüter M et al, systematic analysis of neutropenic enterocolitis in adults, Eur J Haematol 2005 (PMID 16504141); Nesher L & Rolston KV, Clin Infect Dis 2013;56:711 (review); current practice syntheses (StatPearls, Medscape). Antibiotic backbone aligns with the IDSA febrile-neutropenia guideline (Freifeld 2011, PMID 21205990). ESMO Handbook ch. 19.

records.title: Acute transfusion reactions
records.subtitle: Haematological
records.body: Any new fever, hypotension, dyspnoea, rash or pain during or shortly after a transfusion. The dangerous reactions — ABO haemolysis, bacterial sepsis, anaphylaxis, TRALI — present early and can look identical to a benign febrile reaction at onset. STOP the transfusion; keep the line open with 0.9% saline. Recheck patient identity against the unit and compatibility label — ABO incompatibility is a bedside clerical failure. ABC and obs; escalate by picture — IM adrenaline 0.5 mg for anaphylaxis, fluids ± vasopressors for hypotension, O₂ for hypoxia. Return the unit + giving set to the lab; send FBC, repeat group & crossmatch, DAT, LDH, haptoglobin, bilirubin, coagulation, and blood cultures (patient and unit). Recognise — the acute reactions and their tells Acute haemolytic (ABO incompatibility): fever, loin / infusion-site pain, hypotension, dark urine, DIC, oliguria — minutes into the transfusion. A medical emergency. Febrile non-haemolytic (FNHTR): isolated fever ± rigors, haemodynamically stable — a diagnosis of exclusion. Allergic → anaphylactic: urticaria / pruritus (mild) escalating to bronchospasm, angio-oedema and hypotension (severe; consider IgA deficiency). TACO vs TRALI (both dyspnoea + hypoxia within ~6 h): TACO — circulatory overload: hypertension, raised JVP, positive fluid balance, responds to diuretics ; risk in elderly / cardiac / renal patients. TRALI — non-cardiogenic: hypotension, fever, normal JVP, bilateral infiltrates, no response to diuretics ; respiratory support and notify the blood service. Bacterial contamination / septic: rapid high fever, rigors, hypotension, collapse — most associated with platelets (stored at room temperature). Confirm Clerical bedside check first. Haemolysis: DAT, repeat crossmatch, LDH, haptoglobin, bilirubin, free haemoglobin, urinalysis. Sepsis: paired blood cultures (patient and unit) and Gram stain of the unit. Respiratory: CXR to separate TACO from TRALI; BNP and fluid balance support TACO. Manage (per type) Mild febrile: paracetamol; slow the transfusion and observe closely, or restart cautiously if the fever settles and no other features. Mild allergic (urticaria only): antihistamine; may restart slowly under observation. Anaphylaxis: stop permanently, IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (500 µg) repeated every 5 min as needed, O₂, IV fluids, adjunctive antihistamine / steroid; use washed or IgA-deficient components in future. Acute haemolytic: stop, aggressive IV fluids to maintain urine output, support for DIC and AKI; treat as an ABO error until disproven and inform the lab and haematology. TACO: stop / slow, sit the patient up, O₂, IV furosemide; if transfusion is still needed, restart at a reduced rate with diuretic cover. TRALI: stop, respiratory support (may need ventilation), supportive care — do not diurese ; notify the blood service (implicated donor). Septic: stop, cultures (patient + unit), broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, resuscitate; return the unit for Gram stain and culture. Disposition & escalation Haemodynamic or respiratory compromise → ICU. Notify the hospital transfusion laboratory and team early, and report serious reactions to the national haemovigilance scheme (SHOT / SABRE equivalent). Do not issue further components for that patient until the cause is understood. Pitfalls Not stopping for "just a fever" — early ABO haemolysis and bacterial sepsis are indistinguishable from a benign febrile reaction at onset. Diuresing TRALI (it is not volume overload). Skipping the bedside clerical check — the root cause of most fatal ABO errors. Discarding the unit before it can be cultured / Gram-stained. Related: DIC (this module) may complicate acute haemolytic reactions; febrile neutropenia (this module) overlaps the septic differential. Tinegate et al, BCSH/BSH guideline on the investigation and management of acute transfusion reactions, Br J Haematol 2013;159:143–153 (PMID 22928769) · ESMO Handbook ch. 22.

records.title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation
records.subtitle: Haematological
records.body: Consumptive coagulopathy driven by an underlying trigger — sepsis, APL / other malignancy, obstetric catastrophe, trauma; simultaneous microvascular thrombosis and bleeding. There is no DIC to treat without a precipitant to treat. Identify and treat the precipitant now — sepsis (source control + antibiotics), APL, solid tumour. The only definitive therapy. Send a DIC screen: platelets, PT/APTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer/FDP — and repeat serially (DIC is dynamic). Score with the ISTH overt-DIC criteria (≥5 = overt DIC). Support with blood products guided by bleeding + trajectory , not by lab numbers alone. Recognise Bleeding (oozing from cannulae / wounds, mucosal, ecchymoses) and/or thrombosis with organ dysfunction. Suspect in septic shock, acute promyelocytic leukaemia and other acute leukaemias, and metastatic mucin-secreting adenocarcinoma. Chronic compensated DIC (solid tumours) often presents with thrombosis — Trousseau syndrome — rather than bleeding. Confirm — ISTH overt-DIC score Apply only when there is an underlying disorder known to be associated with DIC. Platelets >100 = 0 · 50–100 = 1 · <50 = 2 Fibrin marker (D-dimer / FDP): no rise = 0 · moderate = 2 · strong = 3 PT prolongation <3 s = 0 · 3–6 s = 1 · >6 s = 2 Fibrinogen >1 g/L = 0 · <1 g/L = 1 ≥5 = overt DIC (repeat the score daily); <5 = suggestive of non-overt DIC — repeat in 1–2 days. The score supports the diagnosis; it does not replace the clinical picture or the serial trend. Manage Treat the trigger — antibiotics and source control for sepsis; start ATRA immediately for suspected APL. Nothing else reverses DIC. Blood products only if bleeding, high bleeding risk, or pre-procedure: Platelets if bleeding and <50 × 10⁹/L, or not bleeding and <20 × 10⁹/L. FFP if bleeding with PT / APTT >1.5 × normal. Fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen stays <1.5 g/L despite FFP. Heparin: prophylactic-dose LMWH for VTE prophylaxis in non-bleeding DIC; therapeutic anticoagulation only where thrombosis dominates (Trousseau, purpura fulminans) — not routine, and not while bleeding. Do not chase lab numbers in a stable, non-bleeding patient. Disposition & escalation Haemodynamic instability or major bleeding → ICU. Urgent haematology involvement, and for suspected APL an immediate haematology referral — this is a haematological emergency, not a next-day problem. Pitfalls APL-DIC: start ATRA on clinical suspicion, before genetic confirmation, and support the coagulopathy aggressively (platelets >30–50 × 10⁹/L, fibrinogen >1.5 g/L). The early coagulopathy — not leukostasis — is the killer; avoid unnecessary invasive procedures. Transfusing to a lab target in a non-bleeding patient. Missing APL behind the coagulopathy in a new acute leukaemia. Withholding VTE prophylaxis in non-bleeding DIC. Expecting the numbers to correct before the precipitant is controlled — they will not. Related: febrile neutropenia / septic shock (this module) is the commonest DIC trigger; acute haemolytic transfusion reactions (this module) can precipitate DIC. Levi et al, BCSH guideline on the diagnosis and management of disseminated intravascular coagulation, Br J Haematol 2009;145:24–33 (PMID 19222477) · Taylor et al, ISTH/SSC overt-DIC scoring system, Thromb Haemost 2001;86:1327–1330 (PMID 11816725) · ESMO Handbook ch. 22.

records.title: Hyperviscosity syndrome / leukostasis
records.subtitle: Haematological
records.body: Two flow emergencies — paraprotein hyperviscosity (Waldenström / myeloma) and leukostasis (acute leukaemia with a very high blast count). Both cause visual, neurological and mucosal / respiratory compromise; both need urgent cytoreduction of the offending load. Paraprotein hyperviscosity: urgent plasmapheresis (plasma exchange) and treat the underlying clone — do not delay for viscosity confirmation if symptomatic. Leukostasis: urgent cytoreduction — hydroxyurea and/or leukapheresis, and move to induction chemotherapy; start TLS prophylaxis (hydration + rasburicase/allopurinol). Avoid RBC transfusion until cytoreduced — added red cells raise viscosity and can worsen occlusion. Correct thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy. Fundoscopy, neuro and respiratory assessment; senior haematology now. Recognise Paraprotein hyperviscosity — high circulating monoclonal protein, usually IgM in Waldenström macroglobulinaemia (also IgA / IgG myeloma). The classic triad: mucosal bleeding (epistaxis, gum bleeding), visual disturbance (retinopathy with dilated 'sausage-link' veins, haemorrhages), and neurological signs (headache, vertigo, confusion, coma). Symptoms are usual once serum viscosity exceeds ~4 cP, though the threshold varies between patients. Leukostasis — symptomatic microvascular plugging by leukaemic blasts, typically AML with WBC >100 ×10⁹/L (some series flag risk from ~50–75; ALL and chronic leukaemias tolerate far higher counts). Presents with hypoxia / dyspnoea and pulmonary infiltrates, and neurological signs (confusion, visual change, headache); fever is common. Hyperleukocytosis is the lab finding; leukostasis is the clinical syndrome. Confirm Hyperviscosity: serum viscosity, immunoglobulins / paraprotein quantitation, serum protein electrophoresis; fundoscopy; FBC, renal panel, calcium. Treat on clinical grounds — do not await viscosity if the patient is symptomatic. Leukostasis: FBC and blast count, film, coagulation and fibrinogen (exclude DIC, especially APL), LDH / urate / potassium / phosphate / calcium and creatinine (TLS), ABG and CXR. It is a clinical diagnosis — imaging supports, it does not exclude. Manage Paraprotein hyperviscosity: urgent therapeutic plasma exchange removes the paraprotein (largely intravascular, so a modest fall in concentration drops viscosity sharply) and buys time; follow immediately with definitive treatment of the clone. Repeat exchange as symptoms dictate. Leukostasis: cytoreduce urgently — hydroxyurea can start before the leukaemia subtype is confirmed; leukapheresis lowers the count rapidly in symptomatic hyperleukocytosis (adjunct, with no proven survival benefit) and is avoided in acute promyelocytic leukaemia (worsens coagulopathy). Definitive control is prompt induction chemotherapy. TLS prophylaxis for leukostasis — IV hydration plus rasburicase (high risk) or allopurinol, with close electrolyte monitoring. Transfusion: withhold red cells until the count / paraprotein is reduced unless there is critical anaemia; platelets and FFP as needed for bleeding or coagulopathy. Disposition & escalation Both are haematological emergencies for a monitored bed and immediate haematology involvement; arrange apheresis (plasma exchange or leukapheresis) urgently. ICU for respiratory failure or reduced consciousness. Leukostasis carries high early mortality — cytoreduction and induction must not wait. Pitfalls Transfusing red cells into an untreated hyperviscous / hyperleukocytic patient. Waiting for a viscosity result before exchanging a symptomatic patient. Forgetting TLS prophylaxis when cytoreducing a high blast load. Leukapheresis in APL — it aggravates the coagulopathy; prioritise ATRA and support. Related: TLS (this module, Metabolic) — leukostasis and its treatment precipitate tumour lysis; run TLS prophylaxis in parallel. Leukostasis / hyperleukocytosis: Röllig C & Ehninger G, 'How I treat hyperleukocytosis in acute myeloid leukemia,' Blood 2015;125:3246–3252 (PMID 25778528). Paraprotein hyperviscosity: Gertz MA et al, hyperviscosity in paraprotein-secreting conditions, Front Oncol 2020;10:815 (PMC7248405). ESMO Handbook ch. 22–23 (haematological emergencies).

records.title: Major haemorrhage (incl. massive haemoptysis)
records.subtitle: Haematological
records.body: Uncontrolled or life-threatening bleeding — resuscitate, activate the major-haemorrhage protocol, reverse anticoagulation and get to definitive source control. Massive haemoptysis kills by asphyxiation before exsanguination. ABC: protect the airway, high-flow oxygen, two large-bore cannulae, cross-match; activate the major-haemorrhage protocol . Transfuse in a fixed ratio (~1:1:1 red cells : FFP : platelets) until laboratory-guided; give calcium; keep warm; avoid over-crystalloid. Reverse anticoagulation by agent (see Manage); tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 min then 1 g over 8 h in trauma / surgical / obstetric bleeding. Definitive source control — surgery, interventional radiology, or endoscopy — without delay. Recognise Haemorrhage that threatens life by volume or by site: haemodynamic instability, ongoing visible loss, or bleeding into a critical space (airway, cranium, pericardium). In cancer patients suspect tumour erosion of a vessel, thrombocytopenia, DIC, or anticoagulant effect. Massive haemoptysis (large-volume or any volume compromising gas exchange) is an airway emergency first — a small amount of blood can flood and asphyxiate. Confirm FBC, coagulation screen with fibrinogen, group-and-save / cross-match, U&E, calcium, lactate and a gas; a drug history for anticoagulants / antiplatelets and the last dose. Localise the source — imaging or endoscopy as the patient allows; for haemoptysis, CT angiography and bronchoscopy identify the bleeding side. Resuscitation and the workup run in parallel. Manage Resuscitate: major-haemorrhage protocol with fixed-ratio product delivery (~1:1:1), moving to laboratory-guided replacement (fibrinogen, platelets, coagulation) as results return; ionised calcium replacement; active warming; permissive hypotension until source control where appropriate. Reverse anticoagulation by agent: warfarin → IV vitamin K + four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate; dabigatran → idarucizumab; factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban / rivaroxaban / edoxaban) → andexanet alfa, or 4-factor PCC where it is unavailable; heparin → protamine. Give platelets for a bleeding thrombocytopenic or antiplatelet-treated patient. Tranexamic acid: 1 g IV over 10 min then 1 g over 8 h — benefit established in trauma (give within 3 h), and in surgical and obstetric haemorrhage. Not for GI bleeding (no mortality benefit, increased VTE). Massive haemoptysis: protect the airway (early intubation if flooding); position bleeding side down to shield the good lung; consider selective intubation of the non-bleeding lung; urgent bronchoscopy to localise / tamponade; bronchial artery embolisation is first-line for control, surgery if refractory. Source control is the priority throughout — surgery, IR embolisation, or endoscopic therapy; products buy time, they do not fix the source. Disposition & escalation Peri-arrest — call the resuscitation / major-haemorrhage team, transfusion laboratory, and the relevant proceduralist (surgery, IR, endoscopy, thoracics) simultaneously. ICU / theatre for ongoing instability. Monitor the coagulation and calcium through resuscitation; correct hypothermia and acidosis, which perpetuate bleeding. Pitfalls Crystalloid resuscitation instead of blood products — dilutes clotting factors and worsens coagulopathy. Tranexamic acid reflexively in GI bleeding (HALT-IT: no benefit, more thrombosis). Forgetting the anticoagulant — always take the drug and last-dose history and reverse specifically. Treating massive haemoptysis as a lung problem before it is an airway problem; secure the airway and position first. Letting hypothermia, acidosis and hypocalcaemia set in during large-volume transfusion. Transfusion ratio: Holcomb JB et al, PROPPR, JAMA 2015;313:471–482 (PMID 25647203). Tranexamic acid in trauma: CRASH-2, Lancet 2010;376:23–32 (PMID 20554319); GI-bleed caveat: HALT-IT, Lancet 2020;395:1927–1936 (PMID 32563378). Anticoagulant reversal: ISTH SSC guidance, J Thromb Haemost 2024 (PMID 39029742) — idarucizumab (RE-VERSE AD, PMID 28693366) and andexanet alfa (ANNEXA-4, PMID 30730782). Massive haemoptysis: Davidson K & Shojaee S, 'Managing Massive Hemoptysis,' Chest 2020 (PMID 31374211). ESMO Handbook ch. 23 (bleeding) & ch. 15 (haemoptysis).

records.title: Acute cancer-associated VTE / pulmonary embolism
records.subtitle: Vascular
records.body: Cancer-associated DVT or PE (Trousseau) — high recurrence and high bleeding risk pull in opposite directions; agent choice turns on tumour site and bleeding risk. Anticoagulate: weight-based LMWH, or a DOAC — apixaban, rivaroxaban, or edoxaban (edoxaban only after ≥5 days of LMWH). Haemodynamically unstable (high-risk) PE → systemic thrombolysis unless contraindicated — the bleeding risk is higher in cancer. Before choosing an agent, weigh a GI / GU primary and bleeding risk; check platelets and renal function. For thrombocytopenia, dose-reduce or hold rather than stop. Recognise New dyspnoea, pleuritic pain, unilateral leg swelling, unexplained tachycardia, hypoxia or syncope in a cancer patient. Incidental PE found on staging CT still warrants treatment. High-risk (massive) PE = obstructive shock / hypotension. Confirm CTPA for PE, compression ultrasound for DVT. ECG, troponin and echo (RV strain) identify high-risk PE. FBC, renal function and baseline coagulation guide agent and dose. Manage Anticoagulate for at least 6 months while the cancer is active. Options: LMWH (e.g. dalteparin 200 IU/kg OD for 1 month, then 150 IU/kg OD) — the long-standing standard, and preferred in luminal GI / GU cancer or high bleeding risk. Apixaban 10 mg BID ×7 days, then 5 mg BID — CARAVAGGIO : recurrent VTE 5.6% vs 7.9% with dalteparin (HR 0.63; 95% CI 0.37–1.07), major bleeding 3.8% vs 4.0% (HR 0.82; 0.40–1.69), with no excess major bleeding. Edoxaban 60 mg OD after ≥5 days of LMWH — Hokusai-VTE Cancer : composite recurrent VTE / major bleeding 12.8% vs 13.5% (HR 0.97; 0.70–1.36); less recurrent VTE (7.9% vs 11.3%) but more major bleeding (6.9% vs 4.0%; risk difference +2.9 points, 0.1–5.6), the excess largely upper-GI in patients with GI cancer. Rivaroxaban 15 mg BID ×3 weeks, then 20 mg OD — SELECT-D : 6-month VTE recurrence 4% vs 11% (HR 0.43; 0.19–0.99), but more clinically-relevant non-major bleeding (13% vs 4%; HR 3.76; 1.63–8.69). High-risk (massive) PE: systemic thrombolysis for haemodynamic instability; catheter-directed therapy or embolectomy where thrombolysis is contraindicated — cancer raises the bleeding risk on both sides of the decision. Thrombocytopenia: reduce or hold the dose rather than stop; guideline platelet thresholds sit around 25–50 ×10⁹/L — follow local protocol. Disposition & escalation High-risk PE → HDU / ICU on a thrombolysis pathway. Recurrent VTE on anticoagulation → escalate the LMWH dose; reserve an IVC filter for a genuine, ongoing contraindication to anticoagulation, and retrieve it when possible. Pitfalls DOACs in luminal GI or GU cancers — higher GI / GU bleeding (Hokusai, SELECT-D); prefer apixaban or LMWH there. Treating incidental PE as benign — recurrence risk is comparable, so it is anticoagulated. Defaulting to an IVC filter instead of anticoagulation. Stopping anticoagulation for mild thrombocytopenia rather than dose-adjusting. Related: DIC and major-haemorrhage cards (this module) for the bleeding patient who also needs anticoagulation. Agnelli et al, CARAVAGGIO , NEJM 2020;382:1599 · Raskob et al, Hokusai-VTE Cancer , NEJM 2018;378:615 · Young et al, SELECT-D , JCO 2018;36:2017 · Farge et al, ITAC 2022, Lancet Oncol 2022;23:e334 · Key et al, ASCO VTE guideline update, JCO 2020. ESMO Handbook ch. 2 (Venous Thromboembolism in Cancer Patients).

records.title: Cytokine release syndrome
records.subtitle: Treatment-related
records.body: Supraphysiological cytokine surge after CAR-T or T-cell–engaging bispecifics; fever ± hypotension / hypoxia, usually within days of infusion. Recognise: fever ≥38 °C after immune-effector-cell therapy — exclude / treat neutropenic sepsis in parallel . Grade by ASTCT (see below). Tocilizumab 8 mg/kg IV (max 800 mg) for grade ≥2 (and persistent grade 1). Supportive: fluids for hypotension, O₂; add dexamethasone for tocilizumab-refractory or grade ≥3; ICU for grade 3–4. Recognise Onset typically 1–14 days after CAR-T (often day 2–3), can be within hours with bispecifics. Fever is the defining feature, then hypotension and/or hypoxia. Concurrent infection mimics and coexists — screen and cover. May co-occur with ICANS. Confirm Obs (temp, BP, SpO₂), sepsis screen (cultures, lactate), FBC, renal / liver panel, CRP and ferritin (trend; non-specific), coagulation (CRS can drive coagulopathy / HLH). Continuous monitoring. Grade — ASTCT 2019 G1 fever ≥38 °C (no hypotension, no hypoxia). G2 fever + hypotension not requiring vasopressors, and/or hypoxia needing low-flow O₂ (≤6 L/min). G3 fever + hypotension needing one vasopressor (± vasopressin), and/or hypoxia needing high-flow O₂ (>6 L/min). G4 fever + hypotension needing multiple vasopressors (excl. vasopressin), and/or hypoxia needing positive-pressure ventilation. After antipyretics / tocilizumab, fever may resolve — then grade on hypotension / hypoxia. Manage (grade-directed) G1: supportive, antipyretics, fluids; empiric antibiotics if neutropenic; tocilizumab if persistent / prolonged. G2: tocilizumab 8 mg/kg IV (max 800 mg), repeatable q8h (≤3 doses/24h, ≤4 total); fluid boluses; O₂; add dexamethasone 10 mg IV if inadequate response. G3: tocilizumab + dexamethasone 10 mg IV q6h; vasopressor; ICU. G4: tocilizumab + high-dose methylprednisolone (1 g/day); ICU, multiple pressors / ventilation; anakinra or alternative anti-cytokine for refractory disease. Disposition & escalation G1–2 → monitored ward / HDU per protocol; G3–4 → ICU. Notify the cellular-therapy team and follow the product / institutional protocol. Watch for concurrent ICANS and HLH / MAS. Pitfalls Missing neutropenic sepsis behind the fever (treat both). Withholding tocilizumab in hypotensive CRS. Steroids at recommended dosing do not appear to compromise CAR-T efficacy — do not withhold when indicated. Tocilizumab does not treat ICANS (poor CNS penetration — use steroids there). Related: ICANS (this module, forthcoming) · grade-directed steroid dosing overlaps the immunotherapy-toxicity guidance in Tox. Lee DW et al, ASTCT (ASBMT) consensus, Biol Blood Marrow Transplant 2019;25:625–638 · Santomasso et al, ASCO guideline, JCO 2021 · NCCN Management of Immunotherapy-Related Toxicities.
