records.title: Anaphylaxis, hypersensitivity & infusion reactions
records.subtitle: Treatment-related
records.body: Acute reaction during or shortly after a systemic agent — spanning a mild infusion reaction to airway/circulatory collapse; treat as anaphylaxis the moment airway, breathing or circulation is threatened. STOP the infusion ; keep IV access, call for help. Anaphylaxis → adrenaline 500 µg IM (0.5 mL 1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh; repeat every 5 min if no improvement. Airway + high-flow O₂; lay flat with legs raised (sit up if breathing is the problem); IV crystalloid bolus for hypotension. Adjuncts after adrenaline, not instead of it: antihistamine and corticosteroid. Recognise Anaphylaxis = acute onset with a life-threatening Airway (swelling, stridor, hoarseness), Breathing (wheeze, hypoxia) or Circulation (hypotension, collapse) problem, usually with skin changes (urticaria, angio-oedema) — but skin signs are absent in up to a fifth, so their absence does not exclude it. Distinguish the mechanism — it changes what you do next: Standard infusion-related reaction (mAbs — rituximab, cetuximab; often first infusion): fever, chills, flushing, rigors, back pain, mild dyspnoea from cytokine release. Usually settles with stopping/slowing and premedication. True IgE-mediated hypersensitivity : taxanes (frequently the first exposure, a reaction to the Cremophor/polysorbate vehicle) and platinums — a genuine IgE hypersensitivity that characteristically emerges after several cycles (typically the 6th+ carboplatin exposure) once the patient is sensitised. Cetuximab reactions in the first exposure can be IgE-mediated (anti-α-gal antibodies) and severe. Confirm Clinical diagnosis — do not delay adrenaline for tests. Continuous obs (BP, SpO₂, ECG). Serial mast-cell tryptase (as soon as safe, ~1–2 h, and a baseline at ≥24 h) supports a later diagnosis of anaphylaxis but never guides the acute response. Document the culprit drug, cycle number and timing for the allergy/immunology referral. Manage Adrenaline is the only first-line drug: 500 µg IM (0.5 mL of 1:1000) anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5 min to response. IV adrenaline (titrated, e.g. 50 µg boluses) is for refractory shock in a monitored setting by those trained to use it — the IM route first, every time. Airway / breathing: high-flow O₂, nebulised salbutamol for bronchospasm, nebulised adrenaline for upper-airway oedema; call anaesthetics early for a threatened airway. Circulation: lie flat, legs up; rapid IV crystalloid bolus (500–1000 mL, repeat as needed); refractory hypotension → escalate to critical care for an adrenaline infusion ± further vasopressors. Adjuncts (second-line, after adrenaline): a non-sedating antihistamine and a corticosteroid — they treat the cutaneous component and may blunt a biphasic reaction, but neither is life-saving and neither replaces adrenaline. Standard infusion reaction (not anaphylaxis): stop, treat symptoms; once settled, restart at a slower rate with premedication. Grade No single oncology scale governs the acute call — sensitivity to the airway/breathing/circulation threat is what triggers the anaphylaxis pathway. Retrospectively, infusion reactions are graded by CTCAE and hypersensitivity severity by the Ring & Messmer / Brown grades; those inform rechallenge planning, not the resuscitation. Disposition & escalation Post-anaphylaxis: observe for a biphasic reaction — 6–12 h for a severe or refractory reaction, shorter (≥2 h) for a rapidly-resolving one; monitored bed / HDU if adrenaline was repeated or shock occurred. Refer to allergy/immunology before the next cycle. Future cycles depend on the mechanism: a mild infusion reaction → premedicate and slow the rate. A confirmed IgE hypersensitivity to a drug that remains the best treatment (platinum, taxane) → formal graded desensitisation in a monitored setting, not simple rechallenge — desensitisation induces temporary tolerance and must be repeated each cycle. Pitfalls Reaching for antihistamine/steroid first and delaying adrenaline — the commonest fatal error in anaphylaxis. Giving adrenaline IV or subcutaneously as the default — IM into the thigh is the standard route. Sitting a hypotensive patient up (or standing them up) — can precipitate fatal circulatory collapse; keep them flat. Treating a genuine platinum hypersensitivity as a rate problem — the reaction worsens on rechallenge; it needs desensitisation. Resuscitation Council UK Guidelines for the emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (Whitaker et al, Resuscitation 2021) · WAO anaphylaxis guidance · oncology hypersensitivity / desensitisation literature (Castells). ESMO Handbook ch. on hypersensitivity / infusion reactions.

records.title: Vesicant chemotherapy extravasation
records.subtitle: Treatment-related
records.body: Vesicant leaks from the vein into surrounding tissue — pain, swelling, burning or loss of blood return at the cannula; anthracyclines and vinca alkaloids can cause progressive necrosis if mismanaged. STOP the infusion immediately ; do not remove the cannula yet. Disconnect and aspirate residual drug through the cannula, then remove it. Elevate the limb; mark and photograph the area; do not flush or apply pressure. Identify the agent → anthracycline = COLD pack + dexrazoxane; vinca alkaloid = WARM pack + hyaluronidase . Recognise Suspect extravasation with any burning/stinging pain, swelling, erythema, induration or loss of blood return during a vesicant infusion — symptoms may be subtle and can be masked by a central line. Vesicants (tissue necrosis): anthracyclines (doxorubicin, epirubicin, daunorubicin), vinca alkaloids (vincristine, vinblastine, vinorelbine), and others (mitomycin C, dactinomycin, trabectedin). Irritants (inflammation without necrosis): platinums, taxanes, etoposide — lower stakes but still stop and assess. Confirm Clinical. Record the drug, estimated volume, cannula site and time; outline the affected area and photograph it for serial comparison. Early plastics/surgical review for a large-volume anthracycline extravasation or any blistering/necrosis. Manage General (every vesicant): stop, disconnect, aspirate residual drug through the still-sited cannula, then remove; elevate; do not flush the line or apply direct pressure. Anthracyclines → COLD + dexrazoxane. Intermittent cold packs (~20 min, several times daily) to vasoconstrict and localise the drug — not warm. Dexrazoxane IV for significant extravasation: 1000 mg/m² day 1, 1000 mg/m² day 2, 500 mg/m² day 3 (cap at BSA 2 m²; reduce 50% if CrCl <40 mL/min), first dose within 6 h and each day at the same hour, into a different limb. Remove the cold pack 15 min before and during the dexrazoxane infusion (vasoconstriction impairs delivery). Topical DMSO is an alternative where dexrazoxane is unavailable — do not combine with dexrazoxane. Vinca alkaloids → WARM + hyaluronidase. Intermittent warm compresses to disperse and dilute the drug (the opposite of anthracyclines — the classic trap), plus hyaluronidase 150–1500 U SC around the site to break down tissue matrix and aid dispersion. Cold is contraindicated here. Mitomycin C / mitoxantrone → topical DMSO to the area, air-dried, repeated over several days. Grade No single severity ladder — management is driven by the drug class (vesicant vs irritant, and which vesicant), which sets the compress temperature and the antidote. Severity is then judged clinically by tissue changes over the following days (erythema → blistering → ulceration/necrosis). Disposition & escalation Surgical / plastics referral for blistering, progressive pain, ulceration, or any large anthracycline extravasation despite dexrazoxane — debridement/reconstruction may be needed. Document fully, notify the treating team, and complete an incident report; review with pharmacy before the next cycle (line choice, administration route). Pitfalls Reversing the compresses — cold for vinca alkaloids or warm for anthracyclines worsens the injury. Anthracycline = cold; vinca = warm. Missing the 6-hour dexrazoxane window, or leaving the cold pack on during the infusion. Flushing the line or applying pressure — both spread the vesicant. Under-reacting to a central-line extravasation because the early signs are hidden. Pérez Fidalgo et al, ESMO-EONS Clinical Practice Guidelines, Ann Oncol 2012;23(Suppl 7):vii167 · Mouridsen et al (Savene TT01/TT02), Ann Oncol 2007;18:546 · Savene (dexrazoxane) EMA SmPC · ONS/ASCO extravasation guideline 2025. ESMO Handbook ch. on extravasation.

records.title: ICANS (immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity)
records.subtitle: Treatment-related
records.body: Neurotoxicity after CAR-T or T-cell–engaging therapy — tremor, dysgraphia, expressive aphasia, reduced consciousness, seizures; typically follows or overlaps CRS, days after infusion. Recognise: new tremor, word-finding difficulty or drowsiness after immune-effector-cell therapy — expressive aphasia is the most specific early sign . Score the ICE (0–10) and assign the ASTCT grade (see below). Corticosteroids are first-line — dexamethasone (grade-directed); levetiracetam for seizure prophylaxis/treatment. Tocilizumab does NOT treat ICANS (no CNS penetration) — use it only for concurrent CRS. Recognise Onset usually after CAR-T, often after or during CRS (rarely before), and can recur days later once CRS has settled. Stereotyped progression: tremor, dysgraphia, impaired attention and mild lethargy → expressive aphasia (impaired naming, paraphasic errors, verbal perseveration) → depressed consciousness, and, at the severe end, seizures and cerebral oedema. Headache alone is non-specific and is not ICANS. Exclude other causes of encephalopathy (sedatives, infection, metabolic, intracranial haemorrhage). Confirm ICE (Immune effector Cell-associated Encephalopathy) score, /10: Orientation (4) — year, month, city, hospital (1 each). Naming (3) — name 3 objects (e.g. point to clock, pen, button). Following commands (1) — e.g. “show me 2 fingers”, “close your eyes and stick out your tongue”. Writing (1) — write a standard sentence. Attention (1) — count backwards from 100 by 10. Plus regular assessment of level of consciousness, seizure activity, motor findings, and signs of raised ICP. Neuro obs, fundoscopy for papilloedema; low threshold for MRI brain and EEG (non-convulsive status), and LP where cerebral oedema/raised ICP is not suspected. Grade — ASTCT 2019 G1 ICE 7–9; awakens spontaneously. G2 ICE 3–6; and/or depressed consciousness arousable to voice. G3 ICE 0–2; and/or arousable only to tactile stimulus; any clinical or electrographic seizure that resolves; or focal/local cerebral oedema on imaging. G4 ICE 0 and unarousable (stupor/coma); prolonged (>5 min) or repetitive seizures without return to baseline; deep focal motor weakness (hemi-/paraparesis); or signs of raised ICP / diffuse cerebral oedema (Cushing’s triad, papilloedema, CN VI palsy, decerebrate/decorticate posturing). The overall grade is set by the most severe domain — a normal ICE does not exclude high-grade ICANS if there is a seizure, raised ICP or deep motor weakness. In children <12 the ICE is replaced by the CAPD (score ≥9 = G3). Manage (grade-directed) Corticosteroids are the mainstay — start early; do not wait for a peak. Dosing per ASCO/NCCN algorithms: G1: supportive, close monitoring; consider dexamethasone if not improving, especially with concurrent CRS. G2–3: dexamethasone 10 mg IV q6h (or methylprednisolone equivalent), tapering once improving. G4: high-dose methylprednisolone 1 g/day IV ; ICU, airway protection, treat cerebral oedema and status epilepticus. Seizures: levetiracetam for prophylaxis and treatment; benzodiazepine → escalate for status; EEG for non-convulsive seizures. Concurrent CRS: treat that with tocilizumab ± steroids — but tocilizumab does not treat the ICANS itself ; it does not reach therapeutic CNS levels. Anakinra is used for steroid-refractory disease in some protocols. Disposition & escalation G1–2 → monitored ward/HDU with frequent neuro obs per the cellular-therapy protocol; G3–4 → ICU. Notify the cellular-therapy team and follow the product/institutional pathway. Watch for concurrent CRS and HLH/MAS. Neurology input for seizures, status, or raised ICP. Pitfalls Giving tocilizumab for ICANS — it does not penetrate the CNS; steroids are first-line. Grading off the ICE alone and missing high-grade features (seizure, raised ICP, deep motor weakness). Attributing new drowsiness to sedatives and delaying steroids. Missing non-convulsive status — get an EEG for unexplained depressed consciousness. Related: CRS (this module) — ICANS often follows or overlaps CRS, and tocilizumab for concurrent CRS does not treat ICANS · grade-directed steroid dosing overlaps the immunotherapy-toxicity guidance in Tox. Lee DW et al, ASTCT (ASBMT) consensus, Biol Blood Marrow Transplant 2019;25:625–638 (grading + ICE) · Santomasso et al, ASCO CAR-T guideline, JCO 2021 · NCCN Management of Immunotherapy-Related Toxicities (grade-directed dosing). Post-2016 — not in the ESMO Handbook.

records.title: Severe immune-related adverse event crises
records.subtitle: Treatment-related
records.body: Grade 3–4 checkpoint-inhibitor toxicities that are immediately life-threatening — myocarditis, colitis with perforation risk, adrenal crisis, pneumonitis, encephalitis, myasthenia/myositis; can present weeks to months after starting, even after stopping. Hold the checkpoint inhibitor and think irAE for any new organ dysfunction on/after ICI — the diagnosis is easily missed. High-dose corticosteroids for grade 3–4 (typically methylprednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day; 1 g/day IV for myocarditis ). Early organ-specialist input (cardiology, gastroenterology, endocrinology, neurology, ICU). Steroid-refractory at 48–72 h → second-line immunosuppression (agent depends on the organ). Recognise Checkpoint-inhibitor toxicity can hit any organ, on a delay of weeks to months, and sometimes after the drug has stopped. The crises that kill: Myocarditis — rare but the highest case-fatality irAE; new dyspnoea, chest pain, arrhythmia, heart failure. Troponin rise, ECG changes; high mortality in early series. Colitis — high-volume/bloody diarrhoea; risk of toxic megacolon and perforation . Hypophysitis / adrenal crisis — fatigue, headache, hypotension, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia; can present as circulatory collapse. Pneumonitis — dyspnoea, cough, hypoxia; can progress to respiratory failure. Neuro / neuromuscular — encephalitis; and a myasthenia–myositis–myocarditis overlap that can cause respiratory failure (monitor FVC/bulbar function). Confirm Organ-directed and urgent: myocarditis → troponin, ECG, echo, cardiac MRI (± biopsy); colitis → stool infection screen, CT/flexible sigmoidoscopy; endocrine → cortisol, ACTH, glucose, sodium, thyroid, paired pituitary axis; pneumonitis → CT chest, exclude infection; neuro → MRI, LP, EEG, and CK + repetitive nerve stimulation / anti-AChR for the myasthenia/myositis overlap. Always exclude infection and progression before committing the picture to an irAE. Manage Shared principle: hold the ICI, start high-dose corticosteroids, bring in the organ specialist early, and escalate to second-line immunosuppression if steroid-refractory at 48–72 h. Organ-specific: Myocarditis: methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily (pulse), urgent cardiology, telemetry/ICU; steroid-refractory → second-line (e.g. MMF, ATG, abatacept, tofacitinib per emerging data). Permanently discontinue ICI. Colitis: methylprednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day; refractory or severe → infliximab 5 mg/kg , or vedolizumab 300 mg where infliximab is contraindicated (perforation, sepsis, untreated TB). Surgical review if perforation/megacolon. Hypophysitis / adrenal crisis: stress-dose hydrocortisone first (e.g. 100 mg IV then 50 mg q6h / ~200 mg/24h) and fluids — before any thyroxine, since replacing thyroid hormone ahead of cortisol can precipitate adrenal crisis. High-dose steroids do not reverse the endocrine deficit; hormone replacement is usually lifelong. Pneumonitis: methylprednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day, O₂, exclude infection; refractory → infliximab / MMF / IVIG. Encephalitis / myasthenia–myositis: high-dose steroids + IVIG or plasma exchange ; monitor respiratory function (FVC/NIF) — intubate for neuromuscular respiratory failure. Avoid drugs that worsen myasthenia. Disposition & escalation Grade 3–4 irAEs are admissions; myocarditis, neuromuscular respiratory compromise and adrenal crisis are ICU-level. Involve the relevant specialist within hours, not days. Decision to permanently discontinue vs later rechallenge is multidisciplinary — myocarditis and most grade 4 events are permanent discontinuations. Taper steroids slowly (≥4–6 weeks) once controlled. Pitfalls Giving thyroxine before hydrocortisone in suspected hypopituitarism — can precipitate adrenal crisis. Cortisol first. Infliximab in ICI hepatitis — it is hepatotoxic and contraindicated; use MMF instead. Under-dosing myocarditis — it needs pulse methylprednisolone (1 g), not 1 mg/kg. Anchoring on infection or progression and missing a treatable irAE — and vice versa; exclude infection before high-dose immunosuppression. Missing the myasthenia/myositis overlap until respiratory failure — monitor FVC early. Related: Tox owns the full organ-by-organ irAE grading and management ladder (CTCAE grades, prophylaxis, rechallenge) — Acute carries only the acute grade 3–4 crises; use Tox for the complete grading lens · CRS/ICANS (this module) for cellular-therapy toxicities.
